meta.location: The court of king Noah, in the land of Lehi-Nephi

world_behind.title: The answer they asked for, three chapters late
world_behind.text: One of Noah's priests opened this whole exchange by quoting Isaiah 52:7–10 and asking what it meant. Abinadi replied with the law, then with Isaiah 53 entire, and only now gives the exposition. The delay is the structure: he refuses to explain the good news until the commandments and the suffering are on the table.

world_behind.title: A doctrine of the Son worked out in a colony
world_behind.text: These people had been cut off from Jerusalem for four centuries and from the rest of the Nephites for two generations. Abinadi speaks about the Father and the Son without citing a source. His terms are causal, and he gives them in a single sentence before moving on. He is unlikely to be repeating a formula anyone in the room had given him.

world_behind.title: What Isaiah's runner meant
world_behind.text: In Isaiah's setting a besieged city would learn its fate from a runner arriving over the hills, and the sight of him on the ridge was news before he spoke. Isaiah's line is about relief arriving. Abinadi keeps the image and multiplies the runners.

world_behind.title: Dying without descendants
world_behind.text: "Who shall declare his generation" asks about posterity, and posterity was largely how a name survived. The question in Isaiah 53:8 is a lament. Abinadi treats it as a genuine question and produces names.

world_behind.title: Justice as a courtroom
world_behind.text: The vocabulary at verses 8 and 9 is legal: standing betwixt, satisfying a demand, a claim that cannot be denied. The men listening ran a sacrificial system. The sermon describes redemption as a settlement.

world_behind.title: Little children, with no argument attached
world_behind.text: Verse 25 is a bare statement dropped into a passage about who is excluded. Nothing defends it and nothing follows from it here. Moroni will spend a whole letter arguing the same point four centuries later.

world_behind.title: Why we have any of this
world_behind.text: The court will condemn Abinadi within two chapters. One young priest named Alma believed him, was driven out, hid, and wrote down everything that had been said. The sermon survives because a man in the audience changed sides.

words.text: Placed under, made to answer to. The word governs the whole passage: the flesh is subjected to the will of the Father at verse 2, the flesh becomes subject to the Spirit at verse 5, and subject even unto death at verse 7. Each step is voluntary, and the record uses a word that normally is not.

Begotten, in the ordinary biological sense rather than the sense of forming an idea. It carries the entire weight of the definition: the title "Father" is grounded here on a cause. The next clause grounds "Son" on the flesh, in exactly the same form.

Formal pleading on behalf of another, the act of a go-between with standing to speak. The Son is given power to make it after the resurrection and the ascension, not before. Whatever else the chapter claims, it puts the pleading on the far side of the death.

Offspring, descendants. Abinadi picks the word up from Isaiah, where it names the posterity the servant was said to have lost, and then asks four times who it refers to. The answer he gives is a list of people who were not born of him.
The one who establishes a thing, who gets it started. In this record the word almost always names the devil founding a church or founding murder. Here it names the Lord, and what he founds is peace.

Putting a thing back, returning it to its owner or its condition. The verse applies it to people who died before Christ came "in their ignorance, not having salvation declared unto them," which makes it a word about repair.

On purpose, with the will engaged. It is the hinge of the exclusion in verses 26 and 27, and it does a great deal of work: the people shut out are those who knew the commandments and would not keep them.

phrases.term: God himself shall come down among the children of men
phrases.text: The sentence occurs once in scripture and it is where the whole sermon starts. Abinadi does not build to this claim; he opens with it and then spends four verses explaining how it can be said. "I would that ye should understand" is a request.

phrases.term: The very Eternal Father of heaven and of earth
phrases.text: Amulek will give Zeezrom this exact title, in nearly these words, when asked whether the Son of God is the very Eternal Father. Abinadi is answering a question nobody in the room asked, which suggests the question was in the air.

phrases.term: The will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father
phrases.text: The phrase appears once in scripture. "Swallowed up" is total and it is also passive: the will is not surrendered or matched but absorbed. The verse puts it in the same breath as crucified and slain, so the absorption and the death arrive together.

A position rather than an action, and it is unique in scripture. The verse stacks participles (having ascended, having the bowels of mercy, being filled with compassion, standing, having broken, having redeemed), and only one of them describes where he is.

phrases.term: These are they whose sins he has borne
phrases.text: The clause Isaiah left open, closed with a definition. Isaiah 53:12 said he bore the sins of many without saying which many. Abinadi names them: those who heard the prophets and believed. The seed is defined by hearing rather than by descent.

phrases.term: How beautiful upon the mountains were their feet
phrases.text: Isaiah's present tense turned to past and applied to the prophets. The next two verses run the same line in the present and the future, so the image gets used three times in three tenses before it is finally used of one person.

phrases.term: Little children also have eternal life
phrases.text: Six words, no defence, no condition. It sits between a paragraph on who is restored and a paragraph on who is not, and it belongs to neither. The bare form is the point: nothing is required of the subject of this sentence.
Paul writes the same clause to Timothy, and both use it of God's reliability. Abinadi's use is harder: the thing God cannot deny is justice with a claim on it. The sentence sets a limit.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: Defined by cause
verses.text: Father because he was conceived by the power of God; Son because of the flesh; and the two are one God. Every clause explains a title by naming what produced it. Nothing here argues about substance or nature, and the passage is shorter than the question it answers.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: Two wills, one of them absorbed
verses.text: The flesh yields to the Spirit, the Son to the Father, and the sequence ends with the will of the Son swallowed up. Between those two poles the verse lists what was endured: mocked, scourged, cast out, disowned. The disowning is by his own people and it is listed last.

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: Where he stands afterward
verses.text: Ascended, filled with compassion, and standing between people and a legal claim against them. The passage is a list of completed acts with one posture in the middle of it. He is described as occupying the space where the verdict would land.

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: Who the descendants are
verses.text: Abinadi asks the question four separate ways and then answers it: those who heard the prophets, believed the Lord would redeem, and looked forward for a remission. Then he adds the prophets themselves. A man about to die without children is given a family made of listeners.

verses.label: v. 14–18
verses.title: Four sets of feet
verses.text: Those who published peace, those still publishing, those who will publish hereafter, and then the Lord himself. Isaiah's single runner becomes a relay across three tenses, and the last runner turns out to be the one who sent the others.

verses.label: v. 24–27
verses.title: Ignorance and refusal
verses.text: Those who died without having salvation declared to them are restored. Those who knew and refused are not, and the reason given is constraint: justice has a claim and it cannot be denied. Between the two verses sits the sentence about little children.

verses.label: v. 29–31
verses.title: Their own passage, handed back
verses.text: The sermon closes by reciting the three verses the priests had quoted at him. Almost nothing is changed. Having spent five chapters earning the right to say it, he says nothing new. He just says their words back, and now they mean something.

chapter.title: The exposition finally arrives
chapter.text: A priest asked what Isaiah 52 meant. Between the question and this answer stand the ten commandments, a warning about salvation not coming by law alone, and the whole of Isaiah 53. Abinadi treats the question as premature rather than as illegitimate.

chapter.title: It closes on the words it opened with
chapter.text: Verses 29 through 31 are Isaiah 52:8–10, the exact three verses the priests quoted at Mosiah 12:22–24. Against the King James text the differences are punctuation and capitalization, plus two changes at verse 29. The sermon is a loop, and the closing move is to hand the text back.

chapter.title: Two changes in the recitation, and both are small
chapter.text: "Thy watchmen" becomes "Yea, Lord, thy watchmen," and "the voice" becomes "their voice." The first converts Isaiah's description into an address. At the end of a sermon delivered to hostile judges, Abinadi turns and speaks to God instead.

chapter.title: The rewrite at verse 18 is where the answer actually lands
chapter.text: Isaiah's messenger "that publisheth peace" becomes "the founder of peace, yea, even the Lord." The priests wanted to know who the beautiful feet belonged to. The answer, after three verses of prophets, is that they finally belong to the one the prophets were announcing.

chapter.title: The seed question is asked four times
chapter.text: Who shall declare his generation; he shall see his seed; who shall be his seed; are they not his seed. Repetition is doing the work of argument. Each pass adds a group: first hearers, then believers, then the prophets themselves.

chapter.title: Two vocabularies, kept apart
chapter.text: Verses 1 through 9 are legal: justice, demands, claim, intercession, standing between. Verses 14 through 18 are the language of a messenger arriving with news. The chapter moves from a courtroom to a hillside without pausing to connect them.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: The trial runs Mosiah 11 through 17: the charge, the law, Isaiah, this exposition, the consequences, the fire. Chapter 14 said what happened to the servant. This chapter says who he was and who he did it for, and it is this chapter that the king treats as the offence.

chapter.title: The chapter does not stop at its own end
chapter.text: Mosiah 16:1 begins "after Abinadi had spoken these words he stretched forth his hand" and keeps going with the same argument. The break here is a convenience; the sermon runs to the end of chapter 16.

applications.title: Do not answer the good question first
applications.text: Abinadi held the explanation back until the law and the suffering had been laid out. When someone asks you for the encouraging part, consider whether the answer will mean anything without what has to come before it.

applications.title: Say what produced it
applications.text: Father because of the conception, Son because of the flesh. When a term you use is contested, try saying what produced the thing rather than what the thing is.

applications.title: Notice who counts as family
applications.text: The list is people who heard, believed, and looked forward. Ask who would be on your list if belonging were defined by what someone hoped for rather than by where they came from.

applications.title: Check who the severity is aimed at
applications.text: Those who died without having it declared to them are restored. Whatever severity is in this chapter, it is aimed at knowing refusal. Check whether your own picture of who is in trouble matches that line.

applications.title: Say the short thing without defending it
applications.text: Little children also have eternal life. Some things are better stated than argued, and adding a defence can make a plain claim look uncertain.

applications.title: Watch for the word "wilfully" (v. 26).
applications.text: The exclusion turns on knowing the commandments and not keeping them. Audit whether you judge yourself by the first standard and others by the second.

applications.title: Hand the words back
applications.text: He ends by reciting their own quotation to them, unchanged. When you have earned a hearing, the most effective thing available may be to repeat what the other person already said, in a place where it now means something.

questions.text: What have I subjected to something else on purpose, and what did it cost?
When have I stood between someone and a consequence they had coming?
If someone asked who my seed is, whose names would I say?
Am I among those still publishing, or only among those who once did?
Who am I quietly writing off for something they were never told?
What claim on me is just, and am I asking to have it denied?
